ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Participants 792 participants were recruited through Prolific to complete the online study in two waves.

> Data from 403 participants were collected between June and November 2022 as the discovery sample, and a second wave between February and April 2023 (N=389) were collected as the hold-out replication sample.

> Each participant completed all three tasks in a randomized order.

> Procedure Participants were recruited through Prolific Academic (https://www.prolific.com/).

> Inclusion criteria to be eligible for the study included age between 18 and 65, US as country of residence, fluent in English, normal or corrected-to-normal vision, no color blindness, Prolific approval rate greater than 95%, and at least 5 previous submissions on Prolific.

> The study was approved by the California Institute of Technology Institutional Review Board, and participants were paid for their participation.

> In risk trials (Fig. 1A), participants were able to see the urn and visualize the exact reward probability.

> Participants were given a maximum of 10 seconds to make a decision and were not shown the outcome of their choice to avoid possible influence of outcomes on following choices.

> In the social block, participants had the option to see the decisions from two prior participants, who were actually computer-programmed players with predetermined risk preferences (Fig. 1C).

> After seeing the coin flip figure and the urn configuration, participants had to choose between seeing both players' choices, Jordan's choice, Charlie's choice, or none.

> Participants were given a maximum of 10 seconds to make a decision.

> Additionally, one participant in the discovery sample was excluded given a mismatching age on Prolific (18) compared to what is reported in the demographic questions (17), despite the minimum eligible age being set at 18.

> • H2: Participants are overall risk averse and ambiguity averse.

> Characterize social influence on risk and ambiguity decisions: • H6: Participants are influenced by agents in both risky and ambiguous trials.

> This means that participants were more likely to choose to see other players' choices when reward magnitude was larger (Discovery: b = .33, t(11779) = 8.63, p < .001, 95% CI = [.26,.41]; Replication: b = .27, t(11251) = 7.16, p < .001, 95% CI = [.20,.35]) and when reward probability was higher (Discovery: b = .09, t(11779) = 3.11, p = .002, 95% CI = [.03,.15]; Replication: b = .11, t(11251) = 3.61, p < .001, 95% CI = [.05,.17]).

> Participants are influenced by others, but value their own opinion more Our final set of hypotheses related to the mechanisms, and individual differences, in social influence, that is how participants' choices in the social block (relative to the self-block) were influenced by the social information they sought from other players.

> As a sanity check with previous research on social influence, we first tested whether participants were influenced by other players, and whether that influence applies to both risky and ambiguous trials (H6).

> Finally, the current study used an online task in which participants were not paired with live partners, and partners' responses were pre-programmed.

> H6: Participants are influenced by agents in both risky and ambiguous trials.

> There were 8 catch questions in total in the 15 questionnaires to make sure participants paid attention.

> Participants had a maximum of 10 seconds to answer and were not shown the outcomes of their choice.

> Participants had 10 ) running R version 4.4.1 (also tested under 4.5.2 and 4.6.0).

> C-D. H8 confirmation with computational modelling: Participants are more influenced by the risky than by the safe player.

Ethics approval statement:

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 340 columns across 16 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 16 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: The study was approved by the California Institute of Technology Institutional Review Board, and participants were paid for their participation.
live_data_statements: Participants 792 participants were recruited through Prolific to complete the online study in two waves.

Data from 403 participants were collected between June and November 2022 as the discovery sample, and a second wave between February and April 2023 (N=389) were collected as the hold-out replication sample.
Each participant completed all three tasks in a randomized order.
Procedure Participants were recruited through Prolific Academic (https://www.prolific.com/).

Inclusion criteria to be eligible for the study included age between 18 and 65, US as country of residence, fluent in English, normal or corrected-to-normal vision, no color blindness, Prolific approval rate greater than 95%, and at least 5 previous submissions on Prolific.
The study was approved by the California Institute of Technology Institutional Review Board, and participants were paid for their participation.
In risk trials (Fig. 1A), participants were able to see the urn and visualize the exact reward probability.
Participants were given a maximum of 10 seconds to make a decision and were not shown the outcome of their choice to avoid possible influence of outcomes on following choices.
In the social block, participants had the option to see the decisions from two prior participants, who were actually computer-programmed players with predetermined risk preferences (Fig. 1C).
After seeing the coin flip figure and the urn configuration, participants had to choose between seeing both players' choices, Jordan's choice, Charlie's choice, or none.
Participants were given a maximum of 10 seconds to make a decision.

Additionally, one participant in the discovery sample was excluded given a mismatching age on Prolific (18) compared to what is reported in the demographic questions (17), despite the minimum eligible age being set at 18.
• H2: Participants are overall risk averse and ambiguity averse.
Characterize social influence on risk and ambiguity decisions: • H6: Participants are influenced by agents in both risky and ambiguous trials.

This means that participants were more likely to choose to see other players' choices when reward magnitude was larger (Discovery: b = .33, t(11779) = 8.63, p < .001, 95% CI = [.26,.41]; Replication: b = .27, t(11251) = 7.16, p < .001, 95% CI = [.20,.35]) and when reward probability was higher (Discovery: b = .09, t(11779) = 3.11, p = .002, 95% CI = [.03,.15]; Replication: b = .11, t(11251) = 3.61, p < .001, 95% CI = [.05,.17]).

Participants are influenced by others, but value their own opinion more Our final set of hypotheses related to the mechanisms, and individual differences, in social influence, that is how participants' choices in the social block (relative to the self-block) were influenced by the social information they sought from other players.

As a sanity check with previous research on social influence, we first tested whether participants were influenced by other players, and whether that influence applies to both risky and ambiguous trials (H6).
Finally, the current study used an online task in which participants were not paired with live partners, and partners' responses were pre-programmed.
H6: Participants are influenced by agents in both risky and ambiguous trials.
There were 8 catch questions in total in the 15 questionnaires to make sure participants paid attention.
Participants had a maximum of 10 seconds to answer and were not shown the outcomes of their choice.
Participants had 10 ) running R version 4.4.1 (also tested under 4.5.2 and 4.6.0).
C-D. H8 confirmation with computational modelling: Participants are more influenced by the risky than by the safe player.

info.title: Seeking and integrating social information under uncertainty: the role of decision stakes and risky influence

text.text: Decisions under uncertainty are often made in social contexts.

Yet, theories of risky and ambiguous choice typically focus on individual valuation only, while accounts of social influence assume that social information is passively received or that conformity is a unitary process.

Here, we propose that social decision-making under risk and ambiguity can be decomposed into three separable processes: baseline individual valuation, active social information-seeking, and asymmetric information integration.

Participants in two large online samples (Ndiscovery=394, Nreplication=378) completed a new social risk-ambiguity task in which they first made baseline decisions under risk and ambiguity, then actively chose whether to view the decisions of two other players before deciding again.

We found that social information-seeking increased with reward magnitude and probability, but not with ambiguity, suggesting that active sampling was driven more by decision stakes or social confirmation than by ambiguity reduction.
Social information influenced both risky and ambiguous choices, even though participants weighed their own prior preferences more strongly than others' decisions.

Critically, influence was asymmetric: choices from the risky player exerted stronger influence than choices from the safe player, and this asymmetry was weaker among more risk/ambiguity-averse individuals.
Computational modelling further dissociated overall susceptibility to social information from asymmetric weighting of risky versus safe social partners.

Together, these findings provide a process-level account of social decision-making under uncertainty, showing that seeking social information and integrating it into choice rely on related but distinct cognitive mechanisms.

When making decisions in our complex social world, people inevitably need to integrate the potential costs and benefits (risk), missing information (ambiguity), and decide whether to receive and follow information from others (social influence).
For example, when a product's quality is uncertain, users often turn to comment sections and online forums to consult others' reviews before deciding whether to purchase or not.

Or, when making investment decisions, people may learn about the recent market history, the risk and volatility associated with different investments, and turn to a financial advisor as well as their peers for advice.

Theories of decision-making under uncertainty have traditionally focused on how individuals assign subjective value to risky or ambiguous options (Camerer & Weber, 1992; Ellsberg, 1961; Johnson & Busemeyer, 2010; Kahneman & Tversky, 1979; Segal, 1987).
text.formatted: Theories of decision-making under uncertainty have traditionally focused on how individuals assign subjective value to risky or ambiguous options <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Camerer & Weber, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Ellsberg, 1961;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Johnson & Busemeyer, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Kahneman & Tversky, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Segal, 1987)</ref>.

text.text: In these models, choices are explained by individual valuation processes: transforming probabilities, magnitudes and ambiguity into subjective values, then choosing between options based on the subjective value difference.
However, as highlighted above, many uncertain decisions are not made in isolation, and decision-makers can have agency over requesting or avoiding information from others before deciding themselves.

This raises an important question that is not captured by standard models of decision-making under risk and ambiguity: how is individual subjective valuation combined with both active social informationseeking and social influence?
Computational accounts of risky and ambiguous choice distinguish risk from ambiguity aversion.

Risk aversion is often formalized as non-linear valuation of reward magnitude with decreasing marginal utility (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979), while ambiguity aversion is modeled as a discount or penalty on unknown outcome probabilities (Gilboa & Schmeidler, 1989; Levy et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Risk aversion is often formalized as non-linear valuation of reward magnitude with decreasing marginal utility <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Kahneman & Tversky, 1979)</ref>, while ambiguity aversion is modeled as a discount or penalty on unknown outcome probabilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Gilboa & Schmeidler, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Levy et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The risk-ambiguity modelling framework introduced by Levy et al. (Levy et al., 2010) provides a tractable way of estimating these parameters at the individual level and has shown that while people are generally both risk and ambiguity averse, the two processes are dissociable.
text.formatted: The risk-ambiguity modelling framework introduced by <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Levy et al. (Levy et al., 2010)</ref> provides a tractable way of estimating these parameters at the individual level and has shown that while people are generally both risk and ambiguity averse, the two processes are dissociable.

text.text: This framework is thus well suited to asking how valuation processes under risk and ambiguity interact with social information, though it leaves open the question of how social information is sampled and integrated into choice.
Social information-seeking could be governed by at least two classes of mechanisms.

Recent literature on non-instrumental information-seeking suggests that two main drivers of informationseeking decisions are (i) its capacity to reduce uncertainty (cognitive utility) and (ii) its desirability or ability to induce positive affect -also known as hedonic utility (Charpentier et al., 2018; Sharot & Sunstein, 2020).
text.formatted: Recent literature on non-instrumental information-seeking suggests that two main drivers of informationseeking decisions are (i) its capacity to reduce uncertainty (cognitive utility) and (ii) its desirability or ability to induce positive affect -also known as hedonic utility <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Charpentier et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Sharot & Sunstein, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In a social context, where information is not about the outcome of an uncertain prospect per se, but about what other people previously chose when facing the same uncertain decision, we hypothesized that these two drivers would map onto an uncertainty reduction account and a motivational salience or social validation account.

Under the former, people would seek social information because knowing other people's choices may help resolve unknown states of the worldthis would predict greater social information-seeking under ambiguity.

Under the latter, people want to know what others did when the decisions matter more, either because stakes are high or because agreement from others is more rewarding -this would predict greater social information-seeking when reward magnitude or reward probability is high.

Distinguishing these accounts requires a task in which ambiguity, reward magnitude and reward probability are manipulated independently, and in which participants can actively decide whether or not to see other people's choices.
Once social information has been sampled, a second question concerns how it is integrated into choice.
Research on social influence mechanisms has shown that people adjust their own preferences and decisions towards those of another individual or a group (see Lee & Chung, 2022 for a review).
text.formatted: Research on social influence mechanisms has shown that people adjust their own preferences and decisions towards those of another individual or a group (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lee & Chung, 2022</ref> for a review).

text.text: In the context of risky choice, such influence has been modeled as a form of conformity or social weighting, whereby participants combine their own valuation with social information about others' choices.

For example, one study showed that social information changed people's subjective value of risk-taking behavior by adding value -i.e., "other-conferred utility" -to options chosen by others (Chung et al., 2015), with follow-up work combining this account with heuristic follow/oppose behavior (Orloff et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, one study showed that social information changed people's subjective value of risk-taking behavior by adding value -i.e., "other-conferred utility" -to options chosen by others <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chung et al., 2015)</ref>, with follow-up work combining this account with heuristic follow/oppose behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Orloff et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Another study further aimed to dissociate social influence on risk versus ambiguity (Braams et al., 2021), finding that both types of decisions were influenced by others' choices, but social influence acted primarily via a change in risk, but not ambiguity, attitudes.
text.formatted: Another study further aimed to dissociate social influence on risk versus ambiguity <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Braams et al., 2021)</ref>, finding that both types of decisions were influenced by others' choices, but social influence acted primarily via a change in risk, but not ambiguity, attitudes.

text.text: These findings demonstrate that social information shapes decisions under uncertainty, but do not address the possibilities of more specific asymmetries in terms which or whose choices exert more influence.
This distinction is important because asymmetric social weighting may constitute a separate second dimension to social influence that explains biases in the direction of social influence.

During risky choice in particular, an asymmetry towards riskier behavior could underlie people's tendencies to ignore safety recommendations in various societal issues -health, environment, or finances to cite a few.
Prior findings provide evidence for both general susceptibility to social influence (as described above) and possible asymmetries, but they have not separated these components.
Some studies have quantified or modeled social influence in both risky and safe directions, with some mixed findings.

One study, examining learning about other people's risk preference, reported social contagion from both risk-seeking and risk-averse others, with effects of comparable magnitude (Suzuki et al., 2016), suggesting broad social influence in both directions.
text.formatted: One study, examining learning about other people's risk preference, reported social contagion from both risk-seeking and risk-averse others, with effects of comparable magnitude <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Suzuki et al., 2016)</ref>, suggesting broad social influence in both directions.

text.text: Other work supports a directional asymmetry, with social influence in the direction of increased risk-taking behavior found during peer influence, peer pressure, perceived peer expectations, or advice taking (Ciranka & Van Den Bos, 2021; Gardner & Steinberg, 2005; Siraj et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Other work supports a directional asymmetry, with social influence in the direction of increased risk-taking behavior found during peer influence, peer pressure, perceived peer expectations, or advice taking <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Ciranka & Van Den Bos, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Gardner & Steinberg, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Siraj et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Using computational modelling, a recent study similarly revealed that social influence was stronger in the risky than in the safe direction, captured by greater weight assigned to risky social information relative to the weight of safe social information, especially in late adolescence and early adulthood (Ciranka & van den Bos, 2025).
text.formatted: Using computational modelling, a recent study similarly revealed that social influence was stronger in the risky than in the safe direction, captured by greater weight assigned to risky social information relative to the weight of safe social information, especially in late adolescence and early adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Ciranka & van den Bos, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these studies suggest that separately quantifying safe and risky social influence is important; however, doing so does not necessarily dissociate the asymmetry from an overall susceptibility to social influence.
Thus, an open question is whether social influence can be decomposed into these separate dimensions, and whether they each capture unique individual variability.
A further limitation is that social influence under risk and ambiguity has rarely been examined in a framework that also measures active social information-seeking.
This is important because social information cannot influence choice unless it is first sampled.
The factors driving sampling may differ from the factors governing integration, and whether the two may relate to one another across people is unknown.

Moreover, risk and ambiguity are dissociable forms of uncertainty with distinct computational signatures, with people's attitudes towards them varying substantially across individuals and contexts (Charpentier et al., 2017; Feng & Rutledge, 2024; Kocher et al., 2018; Wise et al., 2023; Zbozinek et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Moreover, risk and ambiguity are dissociable forms of uncertainty with distinct computational signatures, with people's attitudes towards them varying substantially across individuals and contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Charpentier et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Feng & Rutledge, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Kocher et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Wise et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Zbozinek et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Such heterogeneity provides a critical test of whether individual valuation processes shape later social behavior, specifically how people seek social information, and how they are influenced by it.
For example, individuals who are more averse to risk or ambiguity may seek more social information.

Individuals may also be more influenced by social partners with more similar baseline preferences, with risk-averse individuals more likely to be influenced by safe others and risk-seeking individuals more likely to be influenced by risky others (Chung et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Individuals may also be more influenced by social partners with more similar baseline preferences, with risk-averse individuals more likely to be influenced by safe others and risk-seeking individuals more likely to be influenced by risky others <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chung et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, past work has largely ignored individual differences, given sample sizes often being too low to address these cross-process relationships, or separate processes being characterized in separate samples.
The present study advances a multi-process account of social decision-making under uncertainty.

We propose that social decision-making under uncertainty involves at least three partially dissociable processes: individual valuation of uncertain options, active sampling of social information, and integration of sampled social information into subsequent choice.
Within the integration stage, social influence itself may further decompose into overall susceptibility to social information and asymmetric weighting of different social sources.
This framework generates distinct predictions.
If social information-seeking is primarily motivated by ambiguity reduction, it should increase when outcome probabilities are more ambiguous.
If it is instead motivated by decision stakes or social validation, it should increase when reward magnitude or reward probability is higher.
Once social information is sampled, if influence reflects only a general tendency to rely on others, it should be captured by a single social weight.
If influence also reflects selective source weighting, then risky and safe social partners should differ in their impact above and beyond overall susceptibility.
Finally, if social influence is shaped by self-other similarity, baseline risk and ambiguity attitudes should predict which social source exerts greater influence.

To test these predictions, we developed a new social risk-ambiguity task that separates baseline risk and ambiguity attitudes, explicitly measures decisions to seek social information, and quantifies social influence as changes in risky/ambiguous choices after versus before social information, all within the same individuals in two independent large online samples (Ndiscovery = 394, Nreplication = 378).

We also employed computational modelling to estimate individual risk and ambiguity aversion parameters, and to dissociate general social influence from specific and directional risk versus safe asymmetry.
Finally, we leveraged a pre-registered replication approach (pre-registration available on the Open Science Framework: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QPHE3) to ensure robustness of our findings.

text.text: Participants 792 participants were recruited through Prolific to complete the online study in two waves.

Data from 403 participants were collected between June and November 2022 as the discovery sample, and a second wave between February and April 2023 (N=389) were collected as the hold-out replication sample.

After exclusions (see Data Cleaning and Exclusions section below), the final samples were as follows: Discovery, N=394 (age: mean age of the 392 participants with known ages was 34.41 years (±10.99 SD); gender: 187 females, 177 males, 22 non-binary, 3 undisclosed, 5 missing); Replication, N=378 (age: mean age of the 377 participants with known ages was 36.51 years (± 11.49 SD); gender: 181 females, 183 males, 12 non-binary, 0 undisclosed, 2 missing).

The task being analyzed and reported in this manuscript was part of a larger battery containing 3 social learning tasks, 2 short tasks to assess executive functioning, and 15 self-reported questionnaires.
Data from the other tasks and the questionnaires will be reported in subsequent manuscripts.

The three social learning tasks in the battery were as follows: observational learning task to study imitation and emulation (Wu et al., 2024), dynamic trust task to study participants change in money sharing as the partner's reciprocation propensity changes (design adapted from Lamba et al., 2020), and social risk and ambiguity task to study decision making under risk, ambiguity, and social influence (SocialRA, explained in detail below, see Social Risk and Ambiguity Task section).
text.formatted: The three social learning tasks in the battery were as follows: observational learning task to study imitation and emulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Wu et al., 2024)</ref>, dynamic trust task to study participants change in money sharing as the partner's reciprocation propensity changes (design adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lamba et al., 2020)</ref>, and social risk and ambiguity task to study decision making under risk, ambiguity, and social influence (SocialRA, explained in detail below, see Social Risk and Ambiguity Task section).

text.text: Each task had detailed instructions and questions to make sure participants understood the task requirements.
Each participant completed all three tasks in a randomized order.

Two short tasks were added to measure and control for executive functioning: a 9-item shortened version of the Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices test (Bilker et al., 2012) for fluid intelligence, and a digit-span task for working memory (Luthra & Todd, 2019; Woods et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Two short tasks were added to measure and control for executive functioning: a 9-item shortened version of the Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices test <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bilker et al., 2012)</ref> for fluid intelligence, and a digit-span task for working memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Luthra & Todd, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Woods et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Fifteen selfreported questionnaires were used to measure transdiagnostic psychiatric symptoms (see Supplementary Material for details).
In total, the battery took around 90 minutes to complete, while the SocialRA task reported here took approximately 25 minutes.
Procedure Participants were recruited through Prolific Academic (https://www.prolific.com/).
text.formatted: Procedure Participants were recruited through Prolific Academic (<ref type="url" target="https://www.prolific.com/">https://www.prolific.com/</ref>).

text.text: After consent, they were asked to complete demographic questions that included age, sex, gender identity, race, ethnicity.
Then the three social learning tasks in the battery were completed in a random order first, while the two executive functioning tasks were completed at the end, also in a random order.
The 15 self-reported questionnaires were separated and distributed as five groups administered after each task.

Inclusion criteria to be eligible for the study included age between 18 and 65, US as country of residence, fluent in English, normal or corrected-to-normal vision, no color blindness, Prolific approval rate greater than 95%, and at least 5 previous submissions on Prolific.
The study was approved by the California Institute of Technology Institutional Review Board, and participants were paid for their participation.

The SocialRA task had three goals: (1) characterize decision-making under risk and ambiguity; (2) characterize decisions to seek social information, and (3) characterize social influence on risk and ambiguity decisions.
With these goals, the task was divided into two parts, the self block and the social block.
The self block (Fig. 1A-B) contained 120 trials, and the design was adapted from a previous study (Levy et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The self block (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A-B</ref>) contained 120 trials, and the design was adapted from a previous study <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Levy et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In each trial, participants chose between flipping a coin which had a fixed reward probability of 0.5 and a fixed reward magnitude of 5 points, or drawing a ball from an urn.
The urn contained two colors of balls, with one of the colors rewarded.
The proportion of balls with the rewarding color (reward probability) and the magnitude of the reward changed every trial.
There were 60 risk trials and 60 ambiguity trials, randomly ordered.
In risk trials (Fig. 1A), participants were able to see the urn and visualize the exact reward probability.
text.formatted: In risk trials (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>), participants were able to see the urn and visualize the exact reward probability.

text.text: In ambiguity trials (Fig. 1B), a gray block in the middle of the urn hid the division of rewarding and non-rewarding colors, thus making the exact reward probability ambiguous.
text.formatted: In ambiguity trials (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1B</ref>), a gray block in the middle of the urn hid the division of rewarding and non-rewarding colors, thus making the exact reward probability ambiguous.

text.text: The 60 trials of each type (Fig. 1C) resulted from five levels of reward magnitude (5, 9.5, 18, 34, 65 (±0.5) points), as well as three levels of reward probability on risk trials (0.13, 0.25 or 0.38) or three levels of ambiguity on ambiguity trials (0.25, 0.5 or 0.75, representing the proportion of urn that is covered by gray block).
text.formatted: The 60 trials of each type (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1C</ref>) resulted from five levels of reward magnitude (5, 9.5, 18, 34, 65 (±0.5) points), as well as three levels of reward probability on risk trials (0.13, 0.25 or 0.38) or three levels of ambiguity on ambiguity trials (0.25, 0.5 or 0.75, representing the proportion of urn that is covered by gray block).

text.text: These levels created 30 unique risk trial designs and 30 unique ambiguity trial designs, and each trial design was shown twice.
Participants were given a maximum of 10 seconds to make a decision and were not shown the outcome of their choice to avoid possible influence of outcomes on following choices.
The social block (Fig. 1D) contained 60 trials, using the same 60 unique trial designs as in the self block, but each design was only shown once in the social block.
text.formatted: The social block (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1D</ref>) contained 60 trials, using the same 60 unique trial designs as in the self block, but each design was only shown once in the social block.

text.text: In the social block, participants had the option to see the decisions from two prior participants, who were actually computer-programmed players with predetermined risk preferences (Fig. 1C).
text.formatted: In the social block, participants had the option to see the decisions from two prior participants, who were actually computer-programmed players with predetermined risk preferences (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1C</ref>).

text.text: The "safe" player had a softmax beta of 5, a risk preference of 0.2, and an ambiguity aversion of 1.2, while the "risky" player had a softmax beta of 5, a risk preference of 0.8, and an ambiguity aversion of 0.2 (see Model 1 in the Computational Models of Behavior section for more information about the parameters).
The two players were each randomly assigned one of the two gender-neutral names, Jordan or Charlie.
After seeing the coin flip figure and the urn configuration, participants had to choose between seeing both players' choices, Jordan's choice, Charlie's choice, or none.
If any of the first three options was selected, the choices of the player(s) (social information) would be displayed next to the option.
Participants then chose for themselves with the same urn, thus allowing to characterize social influence.
Participants were given a maximum of 10 seconds to make a decision.

Participants received a bonus payment from one of the trials chosen at random after each block ended (meaning one trial from the self block and one trial from the social block), ensuring that the task is incentive-compatible and that each choice is treated independently.
A random number was drawn by the computer to determine the outcome according to the reward probability.
If they failed to respond on that trial, they were informed that they would receive the worst possible outcome for that trial.
Points were converted into US dollars at the rate of 50 points to $1.

Bonus payments for the task ranged from $0 to $1.40; there was also a $0.25 bonus added for passing the instruction quizzes (one for each block) on the first attempt. seconds to choose whether to see the other players' choices, saw the social information (or '??' next to both options if they chose 'None') for 2 seconds, then had another 10 seconds to choose for themselves.
Besides the descriptive text in orange, which was not shown to participants, the illustrations show what the participants saw.

Participants saw the visual depiction of the urn made of colored bars stacked on top of each other, but were informed in the instructions that the urn was made of 100 balls and that size of each colored bar represented the proportion of balls of each color.
On ambiguity trials, they were told that the grey portion of the bar was hiding the true proportions of each color, thus rendering the true reward probability unknown beyond the visible proportion.
Data cleaning involved excluding participants who had incomplete dataset for the SocialRA task, i.e. either did not start the task, or started it but quit the study before the end of the task.
This resulted in 8 exclusions in the discovery sample and 11 exclusions in the replication sample.

Additionally, one participant in the discovery sample was excluded given a mismatching age on Prolific (18) compared to what is reported in the demographic questions (17), despite the minimum eligible age being set at 18.

For both datasets, data was cleaned and analyzed with MATLAB (R2023b, also tested under R2025b) and RStudio ( 2024.04.2, also tested under 2026.01.0 and 2026.07.1 Six mixed-effects general linear models (ME-GLM), all using logistic regressions, were created to summarize the effects of risk and ambiguity on decision-making in the self block, on social information-seeking in the social block, as well as the effect of social information on decisions in the social block.
text.formatted: For both datasets, data was cleaned and analyzed with MATLAB (R2023b, also tested under R2025b) and RStudio ( <ref type="formula">2024.04.2, also tested under 2026.01.0 and 2026.07.1</ref> Six mixed-effects general linear models (ME-GLM), all using logistic regressions, were created to summarize the effects of risk and ambiguity on decision-making in the self block, on social information-seeking in the social block, as well as the effect of social information on decisions in the social block.

text.text: These ME-GLMs also served as data quality checks.

The first two ME-GLMs (ME-GLM 1r and ME-GLM 1a) aimed to quantify the factors driving baseline (i.e. self block) decision making, separately for risk trials (ME-GLM 1r) and ambiguity trials (ME-GLM 1a).

Trial-by-trial choices of drawing from the urn (coded as 1) versus flipping the coin (coded as 0) were predicted from reward magnitude and reward probability (risk trials, ME-GLM 1r) and from reward magnitude and ambiguity level (ambiguity trials, ME-GLM 1a).

Two other ME-GLMs (ME-GLM 2r and ME-GLM 2a) were run to predict trial-by-trial decisions to seek social information (coded as 1 for choosing to see information from at least one player, versus 0 for choosing none) from reward magnitude and reward probability (risk trials, ME-GLM 2r) and from reward magnitude and ambiguity level (ambiguity trials, ME-GLM 2a).

Finally, to assess social influence, ME-GLM 3 was run to predict trial-by-trial decisions to draw from the urn on the social block only as a function of choice during the self block (on the same trial design), social information (whether evidence from the other players was in favor of picking the urn, the coin flip, or neutral/missing), trial type (risk or ambiguity) and the interaction between social information and trial type.

Additionally, to determine whether social influence differs based on whether the social information comes from the safe versus risky player, a final model (ME-GLM 4) was run to predict trial-by-trial decisions to draw from the urn on the social block only as a function of choice during the self block (on the same trial design), as well as social information from the safe player and social information from the risky player as separate predictors.
All ME-GLMs included fixed and random intercepts as well as fixed and random effects of all predictor variables.
All continuous predictors were z-scored before being included in the model.
All ME-GLMs were fitted to the data using the fitglme function in MATLAB.
Random effect variables of interest from the different ME-GLMs were then extracted and used for hypothesis testing.
Two computational models were developed to extract risk and ambiguity aversion, as well as model social influence in a more mechanistic manner.
Model 1: baseline risk & ambiguity attitudes.

text.text: This model only considered the effect of risk and ambiguity on participants' decisions and did not consider the effect of social information, hence it was only fit to participants' behavior during the self block, in order to estimate a baseline value of risk and ambiguity attitudes for each participant.
The probability for participants to choose to draw from the urn was modeled as a Softmax function of the subjective value difference between drawing from the urn and flipping the coin.

text.text: Both models were fit to the data using the cbm toolbox in MATLAB (Piray et al., 2019), and individual values for parameters of interests (baseline 𝜌 and 𝛼 from Model 1; 𝜔 and 𝛾 from Model 2) were estimated and extracted for hypothesis testing.

text.text: Models were found to explain over 45% of the variance in people's choices (Model 1: Discovery R² =0.456, Replication R² =0.451; Model 2: Discovery R² =0.457, Replication R² =0.461).
As a model validation step, parameter recovery analyses were performed for both models.

For each model, we used the best-fit parameter values from the discovery sample to generate data, then we refit that model-generated data using the same model-fitting method as described in the previous paragraph.
Actual and recovered parameter values were significantly correlated for all parameters (see Supplementary Fig. S1 for details).
text.formatted: Actual and recovered parameter values were significantly correlated for all parameters (see Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref> for details).

text.text: The correlations for the four parameters of interest were as follows: baseline 𝜌 from Model 1 (r(392)=0.930), baseline 𝛼 from Model 1 (r(392)=0.924), 𝜔 from Model 2 (r(392)=0.767), 𝛾 from Model 2 (r(392)=0.681).

Note that the goal of the modelling analyses was not to compare competing models, but to capture and dissociate the effects of risk, ambiguity, self vs. social information, and asymmetry of social influence, which was achieved with the two models and with highly recoverable and separable parameters.

Some of our hypotheses (see Pre-registration and replication strategy section below) did not aim to separate risk from ambiguity aversion, but to determine whether general aversion in decisions under risk and ambiguity relate to social information-seeking and/or social influence.

Therefore, to reduce the number of statistical tests being performed, a composite aversion measure called ρα was created to combine risk and ambiguity aversion parameters (α and negative ρ) with the following equation:
Negative 𝜌 was used since higher values of 𝜌 represent risk preference, not aversion.
Thus, higher values of ρα meant higher general aversion to risk and ambiguity combined.
If associations with the composite measure were found, follow-up analyses were then run to determine whether the effect might be specific to risk or ambiguity aversion.
Data was analyzed in two phases, following a pre-registered replication approach.
Data from the discovery sample was first analyzed in an exploratory manner, and findings were pre-registered as hypotheses to be replicated in the independent replication sample.
The pre-registration is available on the Open Science Framework (OSF): https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/QPHE3.

text.text: Our pre-registered research questions and discovery analyses were three-fold: 1.

What are the cognitive and/or computational mechanisms underlying (i) baseline decisions under risk and ambiguity, (ii) decisions to seek social information, and (iii) influence of social information?
How do these processes relate to one another across individuals?
What is the relevance of this heterogeneity to social dysfunction and psychopathology, especially along autistic traits, anxiety and social anxiety?
We note that this manuscript addresses the first two questions, while the third question will be the focus of a subsequent manuscript.
Our detailed approach was as follows.
First, we summarized exploratory analyses in the discovery datasets into a set of hypotheses that were pre-registered with the aim to be replicated in the replication sample.

After posting the pre-registration on OSF, replication analyses were conducted, following the exact same analysis pipeline as described in the pre-registration (and in the earlier paragraph of this Methods section).
This included the same exclusion criteria, calculations of behavioral variables, ME-GLM analyses and computational modelling.
As pre-registered, we focused on replicating only the analyses that yielded significant findings in the discovery dataset.

Furthermore, for clarity, the main text of this manuscript reports the findings that were replicated across the two datasets; and for completeness, the Supplementary Material reports statistics of the findings that did not replicate.

Following the pre-registration, our hypotheses derived from the discovery sample findings were broken down according to our three aims (note, missing numbers correspond to hypotheses that were initially generated but not supported in the discovery sample, so we did not attempt to replicate them in the replication sample).

Characterize decision-making under risk and ambiguity: • H1: Decisions to draw from the urn at baseline are influenced by reward magnitude (>0 effect), reward probability (>0 effect) and ambiguity (<0 effect).
text.formatted: Characterize decision-making under risk and ambiguity: • H1: Decisions to draw from the urn at baseline are influenced by reward magnitude (>0 effect), reward probability (>0 effect) and ambiguity (<0 effect).

text.text: • H2: Participants are overall risk averse and ambiguity averse.

Characterize decisions to seek social information: • H3: Participants' decisions to seek social information are influenced by reward magnitude (>0 effect) and reward probability (>0 effect) in risk trials, and reward magnitude (>0 effect) only in ambiguity trials.
text.formatted: Characterize decisions to seek social information: • H3: Participants' decisions to seek social information are influenced by reward magnitude (>0 effect) and reward probability (>0 effect) in risk trials, and reward magnitude (>0 effect) only in ambiguity trials.

text.text: • H4a: Participants who are more risk/ambiguity averse seek more information in general.
• H4c: Participants who are more driven by reward during decisions under risk and ambiguity are also more driven by reward when seeking social information.
Specifically, the effect of reward probability on information-seeking is positively associated with the effect of reward probability on decisions.
Characterize social influence on risk and ambiguity decisions: • H6: Participants are influenced by agents in both risky and ambiguous trials.

○ Additional hypothesis from discovery sample finding: social influence is stronger for risky than ambiguous trials • H7: People value their own opinion more than social information • H8: Social influence affects participants' behavior in both risky and safe directions, but there is asymmetry in terms of the direction of behavior under social influence, with stronger influence of the risky vs safe player.
• H9: There is an asymmetry in terms of the direction of behavior under social influence, with stronger influence of the more similar player.

For any null finding to be validated across both discovery and replication datasets, we further performed Bayesian analyses whenever possible, using the BayesFactor package in R, and report the Bayes Factor value BF10 as an index for support in favor of the null hypothesis.
BF10 < 0.33 indicates substantial/moderate evidence for the null hypothesis; BF10 < 0.1 indicates strong evidence, and BF10 < 0.01 indicates decisive evidence (Kass & Raftery, 1995).
text.formatted: BF10 < 0.33 indicates substantial/moderate evidence for the null hypothesis; BF10 < 0.1 indicates strong evidence, and BF10 < 0.01 indicates decisive evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Kass & Raftery, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Our first pre-registered hypothesis (H1) was that decisions to draw from the urn at baseline are influenced by reward magnitude (positive effect), reward probability (positive effect) and ambiguity (negative effect).
We tested this by examining the results of ME-GLMs 1r and 1a.

In risk trials (ME-GLM 1r) and in both datasets, both reward magnitude and reward probability had a significant positive effect on the probability of participants choosing to draw from the urn (Fig. 2A-B, Table S1).

text.text: Participants' propensity to choose the urn over the coin flip increased with the urn's reward magnitude (Discovery: b = 1.48, t(23610) = 20.17, p < .001, 95% CI = [1.33,1.62]; Replication: b = 1.32, t(22621) = 19.21, p < .001, 95% CI = [1.19,1.46]) and with the urn's reward probability (Discovery: b = 1.41, t(23610) = 22.27, p < .001, 95% CI = [1.28, 1.53]; Replication: b = 1.33, t(22621) = 20.84, p < .001, 95% CI = [1. 20,1.45]).

text.text: In ambiguity trials (ME-GLM 1a) and in both datasets (Fig. 2C-D, Table S2), reward magnitude also had a significant positive effect (Discovery: b = 2.91, t(23602) = 16.92, p < .001, 95% CI = [2.57,3.25]; Replication: b = 2.54, t(22633) = 17.25, p < .001, 95% CI = [2.25,2.83]), while ambiguity had a significant negative effect on the probability of participants choosing to draw from the urn, such that people drew from the urn less when its ambiguity increased (Discovery: b = -.69, t(23602) = -15.81, p < .001, 95% CI = [-.77,-.60]; Replication: b = -.62, t(22633) = -14.07, p < .001, 95% CI = [-.71,-.53]).

text.text: Our second pre-registered hypothesis (H2) was that participants would be both risk averse (𝜌<1) and ambiguity averse (𝛼>0) overall.

Across both datasets, risk preference (Discovery: M = .42, SD = .35; Replication: M = .47, SD = .51) was indeed found to be significantly smaller than 1 (Discovery: t(393) = -32.22, p < .001; Replication: t(377) = -20.58, p < .001; Fig. 2E-F, left).

Reward probability as a driver of risky choice predicts reward probability as a driver of social information-seeking
We next sought out to examine whether individual differences in baseline attitudes towards reward, risk and ambiguity during decisions predict information-seeking tendencies across participants.

This hypothesis (H4) was further broken down into three hypotheses; that participants who were more risk/ambiguity averse would seek more social information in general (H4a), that they would seek more information specifically when uncertainty/ambiguity is high (H4b), and that participants who are more driven by reward during gambling decisions are also more driven by reward when seeking social information (H4c).
We also initially hypothesized that participants would seek more information from the partner they are more similar to (H5).

We report the findings of H4a in the Supplementary Materials, given that the pre-registered findings did not replicate, while H4b and H5 were not supported in the discovery dataset (see pre-registration for details) and were thus removed from the set of hypotheses to test.

To test H4c, a Pearson's correlation was performed between the effect of reward magnitude on selfblock decisions from ME-GLM 1r, and the effect of reward magnitude on information seeking in social block from ME-GLM 2r.
The same analysis was repeated with the effect of reward probability.

The effect of reward probability on self-block decisions was positively associated with the effect of reward probability on later information-seeking decisions in the social block (Discovery: r(392) = .13, p = .009, Fig. 4A; Replication: r(376) = .13, p = .015, Fig. 4B).

text.text: Related to the novel insights in the mechanisms of social influence on decisions under risk and ambiguity, we predicted that social information would influence participants' behavior in both risky and safe directions, but that there would an asymmetry in terms of the direction of social influence, with stronger influence of the risky vs safe player (H8).

We tested this hypothesis by examining the results of ME-GLM 4, which predicted choice in the social block from past self-block choice on the same trial design, as well as social information from the safe partner and social information from the risky partner as separate, standardized predictors.

We found a significant positive effect of information from both the risky player (Discovery: b = .89, t(23556) = 23.09, p < .001, 95% CI=[.81,.96]; Replication: b = 1.01, t(22524) = 21.00, p < .001, 95% CI=[.91,1.10]) and the safe player (Discovery: b = .19, t(23556) = 6.88, p < .001, 95% CI=[.14,.24]; Replication: b = .60, t(22524) = 16.65, p < .001, 95% CI=[.53,.67]), confirming that participants' choice is influenced in both directions (Fig. 6A-B, Table S6).

Finally, we were interested in testing one last hypothesis pertaining to how individual differences in baseline decision-making might relate to this asymmetry in social influence.

Our prediction was that the more similar player would have a stronger influence on participants' choices, such that those participants who are generally risk/ambiguity averse would be more influenced by the safe player (who is also more generally risk/ambiguity averse), while those who are more risk/ambiguity seeking would be more influenced by the risky player (H9).

641 Discussion 642

In this study, we examined social decision-making under risk and ambiguity by separating three 643 processes that are often studied independently: individual baseline valuation of uncertain options, 644 active sampling of social information, and integration of sampled social information into subsequent 645 choice.

Across a discovery sample and an independent pre-registered replication sample, we found 646 that social information-seeking was driven by reward magnitude and probability, but not by ambiguity; 647 that social information influenced both risky and ambiguous choices while being weighted less 648 strongly than participants' own prior choices; and that social influence was asymmetric, with choices 649 from a risky partner exerting stronger influence than choices from a safe partner.

We further showed 650 that this risky/safe asymmetry varied with baseline risk/ambiguity aversion, suggesting that individual 651 valuation tendencies shape selective susceptibility to social influence.

Together, these findings 652 support a multi-process account in which social decision-making under uncertainty emerges from 653 distinct but related mechanisms of valuation, social sampling, and social integration.

For 654 completeness, our pre-registered hypotheses, and corresponding findings in two independent 655 samples, are summarized in H4c: Participants who are more driven by reward during decisions under risk and ambiguity are also more driven by reward when seeking social information.
Specifically, the effect of reward probability on information-seeking is positively associated with the effect of reward probability on decisions.
Supported Supported samples.
There are two key differences between our paradigm and the literature on uncertaintydriven information-seeking that could explain our lack of finding.

First, uncertainty in the existing literature is usually measured from a known gamble probability (gamble variance, or how close the outcome probabilities are to the highest uncertainty of 0.5), a learned outcome probability (from bandit-type tasks), or subjectively reported uncertainty (questionnaire, confidence rating scale).
Therefore, this raises the possibility that uncertainty reduction dominates over ambiguity reduction as a motive to seek information.

Second, and perhaps most importantly, the information being provided in our study is social information -meaning what option was chosen by one or two other playersrather than resolving the urn and/or providing outcome information.
Therefore, the nature of the information may matter, with social information in our task not actually reducing uncertainty or ambiguity.

Future studies should actively manipulate and/or measure uncertainty and ambiguity to clearly separate their influence on information-seeking decisions, as well as to understand how people perceive a reduction in uncertainty and/or ambiguity when exposed to different types of information, specifically social versus outcome information.

A second contribution of our study is that it separates two components of social influence that are often conflated: overall susceptibility to social influence (relative to reliance on individual valuation only) and asymmetric weighting of different sources of social information.
Prior work has provided mixed evidence about whether social influence is stronger in risky or safe direction.

In late childhood and adolescence, safe advice has sometimes been found to exert a stronger influence than risky advice (Blankenstein et al., 2016; Braams et al., 2019; Ciranka & van den Bos, 2019), whereas in later adolescence and adulthood, this asymmetry might reverse, with individuals becoming less sensitive to safe social information, and risky social information exerting stronger influence (Ciranka & van den Bos, 2025).

text.text: Our findings, related to hypothesis #8, extend this literature by testing for a slightly different asymmetry, namely not which kind of information has the strongest influence, but which kind of social partner.

We show that the risky partner exerted stronger influence on participants' choices than the safe partner, extending the asymmetry from social information (Ciranka & van den Bos, 2025) to social partners, and suggesting that in adulthood, sensitivity to risky influence is heightened compared to safe influence.

text.text: Future work will be needed to assess whether the developmental trajectory highlighted in past work also applies to social partner-driven asymmetry, rather than social information.

Additionally, we found that social information influenced choices regardless of trial types, suggesting that the impact of others' choices generalizes across both risk and ambiguity trials -or known and unknown form of uncertainty, in line with Braams et al. (2019).

(2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, evidence that social influence differed in strength between risky and ambiguous choices was not robust across samples.
Our computational modelling analyses further clarify the mechanistic structure of social influence during decisions under risk and ambiguity.

Previous research has modeled social influence in several ways, including as changes in subjective value (Chung et al., 2015) possibly combined with heuristics (Orloff et al., 2024), changes in risk preference (Braams et al., 2021), or changes in belief about the probability distribution of the prospects (Ciranka & van den Bos, 2025).
text.formatted: Previous research has modeled social influence in several ways, including as changes in subjective value <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chung et al., 2015)</ref> possibly combined with heuristics <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Orloff et al., 2024)</ref>, changes in risk preference <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Braams et al., 2021)</ref>, or changes in belief about the probability distribution of the prospects <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Ciranka & van den Bos, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Our goal was not to adjudicate between these possible mechanisms, but to ask whether overall reliance on social information can be dissociated from asymmetric weighting of risky versus safe social partner.

Consistent with evidence for egocentric discounting found in past studies (Puskaric et al., 2017; Schöbel et al., 2016; Yaniv & Kleinberger, 2000), we show that participants weighted their own preferences more strongly than social information.
text.formatted: Consistent with evidence for egocentric discounting found in past studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Puskaric et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Schöbel et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Yaniv & Kleinberger, 2000)</ref>, we show that participants weighted their own preferences more strongly than social information.

text.text: However, social influence was not captured solely by this overall social-vs-self weighting: our model also accounted for the asymmetry between safe and risky social influence with a separate parameter.

Previous work formally modelling this asymmetry (Ciranka & van den Bos, 2019 , 2025) has assumed that social influence was driven by separate social sensitivity parameters when the social information is risky compared to when it is safe, yielding the risk that while the two parameters might differ from one another to index the asymmetry, they also likely share a lot of variance that reflects overall susceptibility to social influence.
text.formatted: Previous work formally modelling this asymmetry <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Ciranka & van den Bos, 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">, 2025)</ref> has assumed that social influence was driven by separate social sensitivity parameters when the social information is risky compared to when it is safe, yielding the risk that while the two parameters might differ from one another to index the asymmetry, they also likely share a lot of variance that reflects overall susceptibility to social influence.

text.text: Our model is able to better parametrize and dissociate the two cognitive processes, in addition to modelling ambiguity and risk aversion during baseline choices: an overall social sensitivity parameter (ω), and the asymmetric integration of information from the risky vs safe social partner (𝛾).

These two parameters were only weakly correlated, sharing less than 2% of variance, thus capturing two key aspects of social influence under risk and ambiguity and indicating that social sensitivity and risky/safe asymmetry capture distinct components of social influence under uncertainty.

Such asymmetries in social influence may extend beyond other domains than risky and ambiguous decision-making, as evidenced by a recent study showing that during social contagion of cheating, dishonest social influence was stronger than honest social influence (Benistant et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Such asymmetries in social influence may extend beyond other domains than risky and ambiguous decision-making, as evidenced by a recent study showing that during social contagion of cheating, dishonest social influence was stronger than honest social influence <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Benistant et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This underscores the importance of better characterizing these asymmetries and their relationships across domains and across the sources of influence (e.g., information versus partner).
A third contribution of the present study is that it shows how individual valuation tendencies shape later social influence.

Risk and ambiguity attitudes at baseline varied substantially across participants (Fig. 2E-F), as did social information-seeking (Fig. 3A-B) and the parameters capturing self-versussocial weighting (Fig. 5C-D) and risky/safe asymmetry (Fig. 6C-D).

text.text: This heterogeneity allowed us to test whether baseline decision-making tendencies predict how people subsequently sample (hypothesis #4) and integrate (hypothesis #9) social information.
Hypothesis #4 was only partially supported.

Specifically, we did not find replicated support for the prediction that risk/ambiguity averse individuals would seek more social information overall (H4a, only supported in the discovery sample), possibly because the distribution of individual propensities to seek information was heavily skewed (Fig. 3A-B).
text.formatted: Specifically, we did not find replicated support for the prediction that risk/ambiguity averse individuals would seek more social information overall (H4a, only supported in the discovery sample), possibly because the distribution of individual propensities to seek information was heavily skewed (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3A-B</ref>).

text.text: However, we found in both samples that people's sensitivity to reward probability during baseline decisions translated into similar sensitivity when deciding to seek social information (H4c), suggesting that sensitivity to reward probability may generalize across different decision domains; specifically, here, value-based decisions and social information-seeking decisions.

This finding contributes to a better understanding of how informationseeking processes, usually ignored from standard cognitive ontologies (Poldrack & Yarkoni, 2016), relate to other forms of decision-making.
text.formatted: This finding contributes to a better understanding of how informationseeking processes, usually ignored from standard cognitive ontologies <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Poldrack & Yarkoni, 2016)</ref>, relate to other forms of decision-making.

text.text: Finally, hypothesis #9 was also supported in both samples, with the asymmetric social influence of the safe versus risky partner found to depend on individuals' baseline risk/ambiguity aversion.
This association was such that individuals with lower baseline aversion (i.e. more inclined to take risks) also displayed a stronger asymmetry and were more influenced by the risky player.

Overall, this finding is consistent with other studies (Chung et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2016), indicating greater susceptibility to influence from similar partners, whose choices align with one's own baseline preferences.
text.formatted: Overall, this finding is consistent with other studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chung et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Suzuki et al., 2016)</ref>, indicating greater susceptibility to influence from similar partners, whose choices align with one's own baseline preferences.

text.text: Although the present manuscript focuses on links among cognitive processes within the task, this heterogeneity may also inform future work on linking these processes to transdiagnostic symptom dimensions relevant to autism and social anxiety; since both have been related to risk aversion, ambiguity aversion, and social influence (Chamberlain et al., 2013; Chevallier et al., 2012; Fujino et al., 2017; Hedger et al., 2020; Lee & Chung, 2022; Sandhu et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Although the present manuscript focuses on links among cognitive processes within the task, this heterogeneity may also inform future work on linking these processes to transdiagnostic symptom dimensions relevant to autism and social anxiety; since both have been related to risk aversion, ambiguity aversion, and social influence <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chamberlain et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Chevallier et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Fujino et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Hedger et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Lee & Chung, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Sandhu et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: With the heterogeneity of participants' decision-making mechanisms evidenced here, future research can explore whether variation in social information-seeking or asymmetric risky vs safe social influence may help dissociate symptom dimensions relevant to autism and social anxiety, which are often co-occurring.
The current study has several limitations worth noting.
First, the study design generally treated choosing the urn as the riskier behavior.

The risky partner in the social block was programmed to choose from the urn more than the safe partner, with this tendency generated by differences in the two partners' risk and ambiguity aversion parameters.
However, in practice, the urn was not always the riskier option given that the alternative coin flip option also involved uncertainty, with a fixed 50% chance of a smaller reward.

To mitigate this limitation, we avoided labeling the options simply as "risky" and "safe" throughout this manuscript, and instead labelled and analyzed choices as "drawing from the urn" with "flipping the coin".
Future designs could include decision options that more cleanly separate riskiness from reward magnitude, probability and ambiguity.

Second, there were only two partners for whom risk and ambiguity attitudes were confounded, i.e. the safe partner had both high risk aversion and high ambiguity aversion and the risky partner had both low risk and ambiguity aversion.
Some previous literature, as well as our baseline decision-making model, has dissociated the effect of risk aversion from ambiguity aversion.

People were found to be more averse to ambiguity than risk (Vives & FeldmanHall, 2018), and social influence was found to occur primarily through changes in risk, but not ambiguity attitudes (Braams et al., 2021).
text.formatted: People were found to be more averse to ambiguity than risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Vives & FeldmanHall, 2018)</ref>, and social influence was found to occur primarily through changes in risk, but not ambiguity attitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Braams et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: To better dissociate social influence on risk versus ambiguity attitudes, future studies could include a larger set of partner profiles in which risk and ambiguity preference vary independently.
Finally, the current study used an online task in which participants were not paired with live partners, and partners' responses were pre-programmed.

Although the instructions of the social block stated that participants would observe previously recorded partners' decisions, some participants may nevertheless have suspected that partner choices were simulated, and effects may have been larger in a naturalistic live interaction.
Future work can improve ecological validity by using live partners or administering the task in-person, also increasing the generalizability of the findings to real life.

Including other factors that affect social information-seeking and social influence such as social knowledge (how much information one has about the partners), familiarity, perceived partner honesty, and demographic similarity, would also be of interest.
The present study advances a multi-process account of social decision-making under risk and ambiguity.

Rather than treating individual valuation, social information-seeking and social influence as independent, unrelated processes, we measured them within the same individuals and quantified their underlying mechanisms and relations using behavioral analyses and computational modelling.

Our findings make three theoretical and replicated contributions: social information-seeking was sensitive to stakes rather than ambiguity; social influence could be decomposed into overall susceptibility and risky/safe partner asymmetry; and baseline risk/ambiguity aversion shaped asymmetric social influence.

Methodologically, our study combines a discovery-confirmation design with pre-registered replication in two large independent samples, as well as parsimonious computational models that capture baseline decision-making and social influence decomposition.

Together, the present findings support our proposal that social decision-making under uncertainty emerges from the combination of individual valuation, active social information sampling, and selective integration of others' choices.
This framework paves the way for future investigations further characterizing how these processes relate to other cognitive and social learning constructs as well as to mental health symptoms.

First, we found that participants' decisions to seek information from other people, namely to see the decisions of (up to) two other players, were driven by the expected reward probability and magnitude of the varying decision option (the urn).

This suggests that when the varying option is more motivationally salient -because possible rewards are larger or, in risk trials, more probable -people are more likely to want to know what other people did.

This pattern of information-seeking is consistent with a growing body of literature showing that, even when information is non-instrumental (i.e. cannot be used to alter choices), people are biased towards seeking desirable information (Charpentier et al., 2018; Charpentier & Dezza, 2022; Jiwa et al., 2023; Kelly & Sharot, 2021; van Lieshout et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This pattern of information-seeking is consistent with a growing body of literature showing that, even when information is non-instrumental (i.e. cannot be used to alter choices), people are biased towards seeking desirable information <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Charpentier et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Charpentier & Dezza, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Jiwa et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kelly & Sharot, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">van Lieshout et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we extend this idea to a different kind of information and to social contexts: instead of the information being about the outcome of an uncertain lottery, it is about knowing the choices made by other people.
The information is not valenced per se in this task, since seeing the other players' choice doesn't directly convey information about the outcome of the lottery.
Additionally, the social information could be considered instrumental, since participants can use it to alter their choice later on -even though it wouldn't increase their odds.

One possible interpretation is that participants sought social confirmation or anticipated agreement, both of which are desirable and socially rewarding forms of information (Kappes et al., 2020; Mistry & Liljeholm, 2019).
text.formatted: One possible interpretation is that participants sought social confirmation or anticipated agreement, both of which are desirable and socially rewarding forms of information <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Kappes et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Mistry & Liljeholm, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: That is, when stakes are high, participants may be more motivated to know whether others made the same choice, and in doing so increase the likelihood that the social information will confirm their choice.
Whether driven by expected value or anticipated social validation, these findings are consistent with motivational salience as a key driver of social information-seeking.
On the other hand, contrary to our predictions, we did not find ambiguity to be a significant predictor of social information-seeking.

Previous research suggests that information is often sought to reduce uncertainty (Charpentier et al., 2018; Gershman, 2019; Kelly & Sharot, 2021; van der Sluis, 2025; van Lieshout et al., 2021; White et al., 2019), so ambiguity as a form of unknown uncertainty was predicted to increase people's desire to see other people's choices.

Parameter recovery.
To validate our computational models, we performed parameter analyses using participants' best-fitting parameters from the discovery sample (N=394) to generate data using each Model.
Models were then re-fit to the generated data using the same optimization method as for the main model-fitting analyses.
Parameter estimates from the recovery were correlated with the actual parameters used to generate the data, for both Model 1 (A) and Model 2 (B).
Each scatter plot depicts the recovery of a single parameter, described in the plot title.
Each dot is a participant, red lines show the best-fitting line, dashed blue lines are the identity line.
R: Pearson's correlation coefficient, p: P-value from the two-tailed correlation test.
